cards.hyp: Meter on GPIO39 (L RPWM) with RST held reads ≈ 3.3 V (ESP32-S3 boot pull-up); with 10 kΩ from GPIO39 to GND it reads < 0.8 V. GPIO40–42 read < 0.8 V in normal boot.
cards.note: Found in the T3 review. Do it BEFORE the first bts7960 bench run. DevKit on USB only, BTS7960 not connected. Meter DC V, GPIO39 → GND: (1) sketch running, (2) RST held, (3) BUT1 + RST held (download mode). Repeat for GPIO40, 41, 42. Then 10 kΩ GPIO39 → GND and repeat (2). Until this is closed: rocker in KILL whenever you flash or press reset, RUN only after the banner. The result decides 10 kΩ pull-downs on GPIO39–42 in pcb/carrier-revA/SPEC.md and on breadboards 1/2b (firmware/armini uses the same pins). Source: github.com/mcuw/esp32-s3-pinouts. Photo: meter display at each step, C015_NN.
cards.result: STEP D 11.10 ~18:50. DevKit on USB only, `ladder` sketch, which does not touch 39–42. Meter DC V to EXT2 pin 1 GND. Readings (1) sketch running / (2) EN held low (reset) / (3) download mode (GPIO0 low + RST): GPIO39 (EXT2-9, L RPWM) 3.148 / 0.020 / 3.231 · GPIO40 (EXT2-8, L LPWM) 0.022 / 0.020 / 3.236 · GPIO41 (EXT2-7, R RPWM) 0.020 / 0.018 / 0.023 · GPIO42 (EXT2-6, R LPWM) 0.022 / 0.021 / 0.025. 10 kΩ GPIO39→GND in reset: 0, but that says nothing because 39 is already 0 in reset. HYPOTHESIS PARTLY WRONG: in reset all four pins are LOW. The danger is AFTER reset. (a) GPIO39 stays HIGH when the code does not drive it, so from reset until setup() drives it LOW the left BTS7960 sees RPWM = 1, LPWM = 0, which is FULL FORWARD if its EN pins are high. (b) In download mode (flashing) 39 AND 40 are HIGH: both half-bridges high = brake, but the order in which they rise is unknown. Right driver (41/42) stays LOW in all three states. NEXT (5 min): 10 kΩ GPIO39→GND in state 1 and state 3, and 10 kΩ GPIO40→GND in state 3. If it drops < 0.8 V, it is a weak pull-up and 10 k pull-downs fix it. If it stays ~3 V, the pin is DRIVEN, and only gating the BTS EN pins (low at boot) or moving the PWM pins fixes it. Until closed: rocker in KILL when flashing or resetting. 10 kΩ REDO 19:06: GPIO39 in state 1, GPIO39 in state 3 and GPIO40 in state 3 all read ~0 V. So the HIGH is very weak, and a 10 kΩ pull-down overrides it completely. A typical ~45 kΩ internal pull-up would still leave ~0.6 V, so the pins may simply be floating; a pull-down fixes both cases. DECISION (Teddy + Claude 11.10): 10 kΩ pull-downs to GND on GPIO39, 40, 41 and 42 on the breadboard now, on the perfboard (C031) and on carrier rev B (C032). Firmware drives the four pins LOW first thing in setup(). The rocker stays the hardware layer: R_EN/L_EN go through its RUN pole, so KILL cuts both drivers whatever the PWM pins do. SANITY CHECK 19:15: resistor out → 3.2 V, resistor in → 0, so the zeros are real. CLOSED 11.10 19:15 · Partial: the hypothesis was right about the 10 kΩ and about 40–42 in normal boot, but wrong about reset (all LOW in reset; the HIGH comes after it and in download mode). Written into hardware/wiring/PINOUT.md item 4, pins_devkit.h and STATE.md (for Cursor to commit). Was: (1) 1-min sanity check: resistor out in state 1 → ~3.1 V again, resistor in → ~0; (2) optional logic-analyzer capture of 39–42 through 3 × RST and one flash with the 4 pull-downs fitted, no BTS7960 connected, all lines LOW except when the sketch drives them (catches short pulses a meter misses).

So feeding 5 V into pin 21 with USB plugged in is safe: the USB host cannot be back-fed. The other direction (USB on, 12 V off) puts ~4.7 V from USB onto the carrier rail and into the buck output through F1 → add D2 Schottky (SS14 / 1N5819) between F1 and +5V on the carrier; the rail then sits at ~4.7 V, which is what the DevKit itself gets from USB. cards.note:
For C019. The servo stops ~16 mm high: the cable outlet (the black block where the wire leaves the case, at the spline end) sits on the pocket rim, and the pocket has no slot for it (photo C019_01). This card = the prototype fix by hand in the two black PLA brackets from C037. The CAD fix (cable slot in pivot_bracket and in the cam pan block + a FAILS line) is a separate Cursor job.

1) MEASURE, servo out, caliper on the outlet: a = width across the 20 mm side of the body; b = how far it sticks out of the end; c = ear underside → outlet top; d = ear underside → outlet bottom. Photo estimate: c ≈ 8–9, d ≈ 16 mm.

2) MARK with a pencil. Where: the END WALL of the pocket at the end nearer the idler pin (= where the spline goes; same rule on the mirrored bracket). Centre: halfway between the two insert holes of that end. Width: a + 1 mm. Depth: from the top face down to d + 1 mm (≈ 17). Through the whole end wall (~9 mm) to the outside, so the wire leaves sideways and nothing gets pinched under the ear.

3) CUT (Dremel 4000 is on the bench since 13.10 evening, BOM 136–138): bracket in the Multi-Vise 2500 by the servo block, soft jaws or a rag, never clamped on the idler pin. Thin cut-off wheel on the flex shaft, LOW speed (dial 10–15 k, PLA melts above that): two vertical cuts on the marks, stop 1 mm short of the depth line, break the tab out with the flush cutters, finish the bottom with a sanding drum or a file. Glasses on, the wheel throws PLA chips. Without the Dremel: junior hacksaw or a craft knife in several passes. No hot soldering tip for cutting: it smears, fumes, and softens the insert holes next to it.

4) INSERT HOLES at that end: they are 9.65 apart (d4), so only ~5.6 mm of plastic between them. A slot wider than ~5 mm opens them: fine, no inserts at that end. The servo is then held by the snug pocket + the 2 inserts at the far end, enough for C019 (unpowered, swung by hand).

5) DRY FIT: servo in by hand with the outlet in the slot. Pass if the ears lie flat on the block face (no gap you can see from the side) and the wire comes out of the slot freely. If it still stops: the slot is not deep enough, take 1 mm more off the bottom. Then the second bracket the same way.

6) Only after both fit: inserts (ruthex M3, HS-03 ~220 °C). Then C019 goes on from step 4.

Photos: the pencil marks, the cut slot from above, the servo seated (side view, ears on the face). Write a b c d in the result.

BLOCKER FOUND 14.10 while reading the CAD: the arm's pin boss (circle r 12 round the hinge) sits 14 mm aft of the transom pad, the bracket plate is 6 thick, so the boss reaches x = 2 and cuts 4 mm INTO the plate at |y| 12.5–18.5. As drawn the arm cannot be mounted. The 'stop tab' at x = −8 is inside that circle, so it does nothing. FIX (Cursor, 5 min): th_pin_dx 14 → 19 (boss front at x = 7, 1 mm off the plate; lugs 5 mm longer; the duct moves 5 mm aft, fine) + an assert(th_pin_dx - 6 >= 12 + 1); FAILS line 'arm boss collides with the bracket plate (r 12 > pin–plate 8)'. Alternative kept out: circle r 7.5 (4.85 mm wall round a 5.3 pin on a kick-up hinge that takes the grounding hits: no). Then export part = "thruster_bracket" and "thruster_arm" → build/. Both are symmetric: the same STL for left and right.

PLATE (one, all four, ~70–90 g PETG, ~3–4 h): Hyper PETG, nozzle 240–250 °C as for the hulls, 0.2 mm, external spool, CFS off. A fresh PETG spool unless the slicer says ≤ 110 g (the white hull_aft spool has ~130 g). • thruster_bracket × 2: in Creality Print rotate it so the big 50 × 64 plate lies FLAT on the bed with the two lugs pointing up; the four counterbores (6.2 mm) must be on the TOP face, the smooth pad face on the bed. 4 walls, 40 %, no supports, no brim (the pin and lock holes are horizontal through the lugs: fine). • thruster_arm × 2: as modelled (the 50 × 30 thruster plate is the bottom, the two cheeks rise to the pin boss). 6 walls (print list), 40 %, tree supports auto on build plate only: they go under the pin boss, which hangs forward of the plate 17 mm up; the cheek underside rises at ~37° and needs none. Check the preview: trees under the two bosses only.

AFTER (= C005): 4 × M4 through the arm plate into the thruster's brass inserts by hand; the stock screws are 28.4 long and the plate + frame is only ~14.7 → measure how deep an M4 goes into an insert first; if blind and shallow, M4 × 12 from the DSM set. Ø5 rod through lug–cheek–cheek–lug: must turn freely (ream 5.3 with the rod if tight). M3 lock pin through lug + cheek in the deployed hole. Bracket on the transom pad: 4 × M3 into the pad's blind inserts (same insert routine as the rim bosses). Photos: the plate from above, the arm on the thruster with the 4 screws, the swing deployed → stowed.

cards.hyp: The Ø5 rod turns freely in lug–cheek–cheek–lug; the arm swings −32° deployed → +100° stowed by hand; the M3 lock pin goes through lug + cheek in the deployed hole; 4 × M4 hold the thruster on the arm plate with no gap.
cards.note: C005 with the printed C041 parts (PETG). ORDER: (1) M4 depth: screw one stock M4 (28.4 long) into a thruster insert by hand and count turns / measure how far it goes; if it bottoms before ~10 mm the insert is blind → M4 × 12 from the DSM set (plate 5 + frame ~9.7). Never force a long screw into a blind insert: it cracks the thruster boss. (2) Thruster on the arm: 4 × M4 through the 50 × 30 plate, cross pattern, hand-tight. (3) Hinge: push the Ø5 rod (60 mm, 5 mm aluminium) through lug – cheek – cheek – lug. It must turn freely; if the 5.3 holes are tight, ream by twisting the rod with a drop of water, or run the 5 mm bit through each hole. R-clip (or a 2 mm pin) at both ends. (4) Lock pin: M3 × 20 (or the 3 mm rod) through lug + cheek at r 10 in the deployed hole (−32°); the stowed hole is +68°. Check both. (5) Bracket on the hull: 4 × ruthex M3 into the transom pad's blind holes (HS-03 at 220 °C, chamfer first, flush), then 4 × M3 × 10 through the 6.2 × 3 counterbores. The bracket plate must sit flat on the pad; if it rocks, find the high spot (brim remnant / elephant foot) and scrape. (6) Swing test by hand: deployed against the stop, kick up to +100°, back down; the duct must clear the hull bottom and the transom at every angle. Then the same on the other hull. Photos: screw depth with the caliper, hinge with the rod, deployed + stowed from the side (★), both hulls from behind.

analyses.challenge: The boat's whole premise is finding a person in water with a low-cost thermal array (MLX90640 / 90642). Testing it needs a repeatable target: a 1:9 figure that floats head-out, stays near 37 °C at the head for 20+ minutes in cold water, survives the lift, and is cheap to rebuild. Scaling is the catch — a 1:9 head has 1/81 of the area, so at 1 m the camera sees a few warm pixels, not a face.
analyses.decision: Warm pack now (the v1 video) and a measured bench test (C029: Pesho at 37 °C from 1 m) with the angular size written down. For the real-water phase add a full-size warm target, so the detection numbers mean something at 1:1.

impact.note: Drowning is a leading cause of accidental death; a cheap detector that works at night is direct nature & people impact. Financial: a real product niche. Scientific: new numbers for low-cost arrays.

analyses.lesson: A scaled demonstrator scales geometry, not physics: thermal contrast, pixel size and water cooling do not scale with the hull. Say which numbers are 1:9 and which are 1:1.

analyses.title: Pesho — a 1:9 warm dummy for testing thermal detection of a person in water
analyses.why: The research thread with the most people-impact: how far can a sub-100 € thermal array detect a head in water at night, as a function of water temperature, wind and sea state? The AmphiReach paper assumed it; AR-Mini can measure it. It is also the one line that could become a product (a thermal person-in-water alarm for lifeguard boats) — judge that after the numbers. Patent: unlikely (prior art in SAR imaging). Publication and a competition entry: yes.

analyses.challenge: A 100 × 80 carrier that must fit four off-the-shelf boards (DevKit-Lipo, a PCA9685 clone, BNO055, two JST fields) with no vendor footprint for the clone, in one order, with no time for a second spin before 29.10. Four real-part measurements changed the design on 13.10; on 15.10 real pins did not fit the 1:1 print — the PCA9685 rows were 1.6 mm short because a caliper reading had been 'corrected' wrongly (FAILS 152).
analyses.decision: Measure, cross-check with a photo, print 1:1, push pins — only then order; standoff holes Ø3.0 so M2.5 screws tolerate ±0.2 mm. The datasheets (NXP + Adafruit) changed nothing on the copper, only solder-time values (R10 1 k, LED resistors, the V+ capacitor).

impact.note: Fewer scrapped boards and re-orders in student labs; tiny but positive.

analyses.lesson: Every number that becomes copper needs two independent routes to it. 'Looks right' is not a check; pins through paper is.

analyses.challenge: Two 12 V thrusters hang below the hull of a boat that is meant to drive onto a shore. They must hold full forward thrust rigidly, allow reverse, and survive grounding without breaking the hull or the mount. v1 has no actuator budget for them and the parts must print in PETG. The first CAD had the hinge boss cutting 4 mm into the bracket plate (FAILS 151) — caught before printing.
analyses.decision: Option 3 for v1: the only one that costs no mass, no electronics and no seal, and it tells the story (grounding → kick-up) on video. The price: autonomous runs are forward-only with the pins out. A spring (option 2) is the natural v2 upgrade — it keeps the passive kick-up and buys reverse without a pin.

impact.note: A rescue craft that survives beaching finishes more missions — real but indirect nature & people impact. Scientific: incremental. Financial: a parts kit at best.

analyses.lesson: Mechanisms first, actuators last: a passive hinge that uses the thrust itself as the clamping force solved three requirements at once. And every hinge gets a clearance assert in CAD before it gets a print.

options.what: Rigid mount with a sacrificial shear pin — simplest, but a sheared pin ends the mission and the duct still takes the hit

options.what: Spring-loaded tilt (outboard-motor style): a spring holds the leg down, grounding overcomes it, it returns by itself; reverse works up to the spring preload

options.what: Passive kick-up with a lock pin: forward thrust presses the arm on a stop, grounding lifts it, a pin locks it for reverse, stowed by hand — no spring, no actuator, 96 g PETG

Tunnel or ducted thrusters inside the hull — nothing exposed, but poor low-speed efficiency and a much more complex hull print
Water-jet drive — no exposed propeller at all, but cost, weight and efficiency do not fit a 1:9 demonstrator
